summary:
Existing lunar tools treat each landing site and date as a separate lookup or are too complicated to read. MoonFromEarth starts from the mission instead. A planner states the stay length and the sunlight, Earth visibility and darkness the mission can accept, and the tool checks 18 south pole sites, as well as custom coordinates, hour by hour from 2027 to 2040 and returns the sites and arrival dates that work.

It is built on NASA/JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions and LRO LOLA terrain. One table compares every site by sunlight (power), Earth visibility (radio) or both. Selecting a site and hour shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain skyline, with solar elevation and countdowns to sunset and Earthset, so each number has a visible reason.

The reason matters. A ridge near Shackleton is sunlit for 90.6% of 2027, yet it goes dark for 162 hours straight in May, a point 2.1 km away gets no Sun at all that month. A guided tour led by Selini, a small astronaut guide, walks educators and the public through it in five steps. Planners also get share links and CSV export.

Results describe Sun and Earth visibility only. Power budgets, radio performance and landing safety are outside its scope.
details:
Problem and approach

A lunar location cannot be understood from a map position or an annual sunlight percentage alone. A solar-powered mission needs to know when sunlight is available, how long each dark spell lasts and when Earth is visible for a direct radio link, and at the south pole those conditions change sharply between points a couple of kilometers apart and from one month to the next. Timing decides everything.

The challenge names complicated interfaces as the barrier, with existing tools each site and date is a separate lookup. MoonFromEarth turns the question around. A planner states what the mission needs, and the tool searches 18 south pole sites across 14 years of hourly data for the places and arrival dates that fit. An educator opens a guided tour and sees why two points 2.1 km apart have opposite lighting.

The table compares sites and dates, and the sky view shows the physical reason behind each number. The mission planner then checks a whole stay against explicit requirements.

Comparing sites and dates

The table is the comparison tool. Prepared sites are shown against the same month in separate lanes for sunlight and Earth visibility, and any day can be opened to inspect its hours. Sorting follows the priority of the mission:

  • Power: most hours with some sunlight.
  • Comms: most hours with Earth visible.
  • Both: most hours when the Sun and Earth are visible together.

Selecting a site and an hour updates a horizon panorama that draws the Sun and Earth against the skyline, charts of how far each body clears the terrain, and countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset. The site card gives the solar elevation angle and the height of the Sun above the terrain in degrees, with the same two figures for Earth. Playback and a slider show how conditions change over a lunar day. Hence every number in the table has a physical explanation one click away.

The selected-site card adds terrain context: slope from a 30 m LOLA grid, distance to the nearest mapped permanently shadowed region larger than 1 square kilometer, and sunlight at observer heights of 2 m and 10 m for 2027-2030.

Users can choose a prepared site, enter coordinates or click empty ground on the polar map. The prepared sites include the IM-2 landing site at Mons Mouton, a CLPS mission target, and three Artemis III candidate regions. Five past landings give context on the same dates: Apollo 11, Blue Ghost Mission 1, SLIM, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang'e 6. However, custom and past-landing points are evaluated on a smooth Moon without local terrain, so they are labeled and listed apart from the terrain-aware south pole sites.

The mission planner

A site that looks good on one day can still fail a mission that lasts for weeks. This is where the mission planner comes into play. It answers one question: which prepared locations have an arrival time that meets the requirements of the mission.

Users set the length of stay, the minimum share of that stay with the Sun visible, the minimum share with Earth visible and the longest continuous darkness allowed. Three editable presets give a starting point. Two take their length from real missions, 14 days for Blue Ghost Mission 1 and 100 days with at most 50 hours of darkness for the VIPER plan, while the remaining thresholds are the team's own planning assumptions.

The planner checks every candidate arrival hour, including sunlight at arrival and enough remaining data for the whole stay. It ranks terrain-aware sites by the number of days containing at least one qualifying arrival hour, and shows the next qualifying time alongside a 14-year timeline of eligible days. A slip margin shows how many days the arrival can move and still qualify. That is the question a planner asks when a launch date slips.

The search is an explicit numerical calculation, every result can be traced to the requirements and the hourly data. No AI model produces the ranking.

Example: a 14-day stay in May 2027

The Short lander preset asks for a 14-day stay with the Sun visible for at least 80% of its hours, Earth visible for at least 50%, no continuous darkness longer than 24 hours and sunlight at arrival.

For an arrival at 00:00 UTC on 1 May 2027, the 336-hour stay ends at 00:00 UTC on 15 May, excluding that endpoint. Running the planner calculation on the committed hourly records gives the following for the lit ridge near Shackleton and for the best-lit point on Connecting Ridge, 1.1 km away:

  • Sun visible: 296 h (88.1%) on the Shackleton ridge, 230 h (68.5%) on Connecting Ridge.
  • Earth visible: 300 h (89.3%) at both points.
  • Longest darkness during the stay: 21 h on the Shackleton ridge, 81 h on Connecting Ridge.
  • Sun visible at arrival: yes on the Shackleton ridge, no on Connecting Ridge.

Both points have the same Earth-visibility hours for this stay, so the radio link does not separate them. The Connecting Ridge point fails the sunlight threshold and the darkness threshold, and it has no sunlight at arrival. The Shackleton ridge meets every condition.

The coordinates are latitude -89.43865, longitude -137.49989 for the Shackleton ridge and latitude -89.4739, longitude -137.3158 for Connecting Ridge, in degrees with east-positive longitude.

Example: two points 2.1 km apart

The Shackleton ridge and a shadowed point at latitude -89.36899, longitude -136.5882 are about 2.1 km apart. For May 2027 both use the same 2 m observer height, the same terrain method and the same UTC window, 1 May 00:00 through 31 May 23:00, which is 744 hourly samples.

  • Sun visible: 512 h (68.8%) on the ridge, 0 h at the shadowed point.
  • Earth visible: 457 h (61.4%) on the ridge, 0 h at the shadowed point.
  • Sun and Earth visible together: 436 h (58.6%) on the ridge, 0 h at the shadowed point.
  • Longest dark interval within the month: 162 h (6.75 days) on the ridge, all 744 h at the shadowed point.

Across 2027 the ridge has sunlight at 7,936 of 8,760 hourly samples (90.6%), a figure that looks safe and is dangerously incomplete, because it still contains the 162-hour dark interval in May. Location, total availability and uninterrupted availability are separate questions. A mission window has to be checked against all of them.

Guided tour

The guided tour tells that story in five steps and ends at Apollo 11 for contrast. Each step selects the site and month it talks about, the part of the page it points at stays lit while the rest dims, and on a laptop screen the tour card moves next to it. Selini, a small astronaut guide, stands by the card, greets the visitor and points to the About page at the end. A test recomputes every number in the tour text from the data files.

Every panel carries a one-sentence caption, and the About panel explains how to read the screen. Share links preserve a selected site and time. CSV export gives the hourly data of a site for inspection.

NASA data and method

NASA/JPL Horizons supplies the hourly directions of the Sun and Earth at each site, along with the sub-solar point, the sub-Earth point and the Earth-Moon distance used for custom points. Horizons computes each position for the site and the hour, so the Moon's libration and orbital variation are already included. In turn, Earth's path in the sky shifts from month to month.

LRO LOLA DEM v4 south pole elevation models, downloaded through NASA Moon Trek, supply the surrounding terrain: LRO_LOLA_DEM_SPole875_5mp_v04.tif at 5 m per pixel and LRO_LOLA_DEM_SPole75_30mp_v04.tif at 30 m per pixel.

The team calculates a skyline in 360 directions around each prepared point, accounting for lunar curvature, with the 5 m or 30 m terrain near the site and a coarser representation farther away, out to 150 km. The standard observer stands 2 m above local ground. A body counts as visible at a sampled hour when any part of its apparent disc clears the terrain horizon, and no atmospheric refraction is applied because the Moon has no atmosphere.

Those calculations become hourly records and daily summaries, which the website turns into the table, the panorama, the charts and the mission-window search. NASA data drives both the comparison and its explanation. The site selection and the processing workflow are the team's contribution.

The prepared dataset contains 18 terrain-aware south pole points with hourly data for 2027-2040. LOLA also supplies the map relief and the ground slope. Distances to large permanent shadows use NASA PGDA's LOLA polygon product LPSR_80S_20MPP_ADJ_1km2, with Barker et al. (2023) credited for the data, and NASA NSSDCA's Table of Anthropogenic Impacts and Spacecraft on the Moon supplies the coordinates of the five past landings.

Validation and limits

The repository includes checks for coverage, for visibility values and for agreement between hourly and daily totals. The May totals above were recounted from the committed hourly records, and the 14-day example uses the same calculation as the implemented planner.

Separate pipeline benchmarks are compared with the Connecting Ridge study published by Gläser and colleagues. At two published locations with a 10 m observer, the project's 2027 sunlit fractions differ from the reported multi-year results by about 0.3-0.4 percentage points. At the two 2 m benchmark locations the differences are larger, about 5.6 and 8.1 points. A further check that takes the maximum within a 20 m neighborhood still leaves gaps of approximately 5.1 and 5.3 points at 2 m. It does not resolve the discrepancy. Terrain products and time coverage differ between the two studies, the cause has not been established. Hence these comparisons do not establish a general accuracy percentage or a complete replication.

The results have the following limits:

  • Visibility only. Sun visibility is not an electrical-power or thermal calculation. Earth visibility is not a radio-link budget and does not confirm that a particular ground station can communicate.
  • Model outputs. The results are simulated and were never observed. Hourly sampling and finite terrain resolution limit precision, and terrain errors are not propagated.
  • Team-computed points. The computed sites come from the team's terrain scan. NASA has not designated them as landing sites, and a region center does not describe every location in its region.
  • No suitability score. Sort labels and planner results describe modeled visibility. They do not assess every terrain hazard, spacecraft constraint or trajectory needed to approve a landing. Planner presets are editable assumptions, and the slip margin is flexibility inside the visibility window, with no launch-trajectory calculation behind it.
  • Terrain indicators. Slope describes terrain at a 30 m scale and says nothing about roughness beneath a lander. The shadow-distance product excludes shadows smaller than 1 square kilometer and does not confirm water ice. A point shadowed in the simulation is not automatically permanently shadowed. The map relief uses illustrative lighting, which is different from real-time sunlight.
  • Smooth-Moon points. Custom and past-landing points have no local terrain and are never ranked against the terrain-aware sites.
  • Year boundaries. Stored annual summaries cut a dark spell at each New Year. The selected-site verdict and the planner use joined hourly data, so a spell across New Year stays whole. Spells are still cut at the start of 2027 and the end of 2040.
  • Not yet measured. Educational outcomes, task-time improvements and professional adoption.

Tools

The website uses Next.js, React and TypeScript with Tailwind and shadcn/ui components. Python prepares the scientific data. The next steps are further validation at the standard 2 m height and observation of first-time users.

Source code: https://github.com/nitrimandylis/moon-from-earth

Use of AI tools

AI tools assisted the team throughout the project. Claude Code (Anthropic) assisted with writing and editing the website, the data-processing scripts, the tests and the documentation, working from the team's instructions. The slide deck was also made with Claude: the team chose the story, the slide split and the wording, while Claude Code captured the screenshots from the site and laid out the slides. The automated pull-request review uses Claude Code as well, after deterministic checks. The Claude models used were Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. ChatGPT and Codex (OpenAI) assisted with reading the rules, source synthesis and drafting this submission text, using GPT-6.1 Sol, and Claude Code then revised the text.

The scientific workflow uses NASA positions and terrain. Table sorting and mission-window rankings are explicit numerical calculations, no AI model runs when the website is used.

One image is AI-generated: the team logo on slide 1 of the deck, made with GPT Image 2 and carrying a visible "AI-generated" mark. Selini, the astronaut tour guide, did not come from an image model. It is a vector drawing written as code with Claude Code, acknowledged like the rest of the code. There is no AI-generated video or audio, and the map relief is computed from LOLA data.

The team chose the sites, the features and the story, tested each feature in the browser and read the results and benchmark tables. The team did not read every line of generated code, automated tests and a benchmark against published results cover the rest. The repository README and story/sources.md carry the same acknowledgment.
